# Results

What the system measured, how different that is from what it replaced or what it is compared against, and how far to trust it.

## Read this first

**Every number on this page comes from simulated data.** Thefts, vacant houses and the network around them are generated by `simulator/`, which was compared with real London households and calibrated against them, but is still distinguishable from real data (a classifier tells them apart with AUC 0.98). No real theft labels were available, no utility data was used, and nothing here was run in the field. Read the numbers as **method validation: how well the approach finds authored thefts among authored decoys**, not as the recovery rate a utility would see.

Two further things to keep in mind:

- The feeder forecast is the exception. It is benchmarked on real smart-meter households, but those are London homes summed into pseudo-feeders, not Indian feeders.
- Figures are taken from `evals/results/*.json`, from the committed docs that cite them, or from git history. Where a figure comes from somewhere else it is labelled.

## 1. Evaluation setup

### Detection

| Item | Setting |
|---|---|
| Network per run | 8 transformers x 6 meters = 48 meters, 60 days, 15-minute readings |
| Injected thefts | 11 per network, placed on random meters: hook bypass 50%, gradual tampering 30%, meter stopped 20% of draws; start day 18 to 40 |
| Injected decoys | 4 vacant houses per network (consumption falls 70% to 95%, no theft) |
| Development seeds | 0 to 19: used to choose the 0.50 flag threshold and to tune the layers |
| Held-out seeds | **1000 to 1019**: 20 networks the detector was never tuned on. Source of every held-out figure below |
| Simulator for the committed result | the original simulator (no realism knobs) |
| Unit of analysis | a meter on the final day. Positives are the 11 injected thefts; the 4 decoys count as false alarms if flagged |
| Metrics | precision (flagged meters that were thefts), recall (thefts flagged), F1, precision at 10 (thefts among the 10 top-ranked meters), per-kind recall, share of decoys flagged |
| Aggregation | mean over the 20 networks, with min and max; 95% intervals derived from the 20 per-network values |
| Reproduce | `python evals/detection_eval.py --simulator original --networks 20 --first-seed 1000` regenerates `evals/results/detection.json` exactly |

220 thefts and 80 decoys in total (20 networks).

### AI features

Cause and answer quality are scored on three unseen networks (seeds 2000 to 2002). The inspection brief is run on every flagged meter and every decoy (41 cases), and its named cause is compared with the simulator's true cause (hook bypass, gradual tampering, meter stopped; vacancy and false alarms should be "genuine drop"). The copilot gets 10 templated questions per network (30 in total) whose answers are computed from the same data; an answer passes if it contains the expected value and fails if it names a meter that does not exist. `python evals/ai_eval.py --mode rules|agent`.

### Forecast and simulator realism

Both use the London Smart Meters dataset (Zenodo 4656091, CC BY 4.0). Full setup is in [FORECAST_BENCHMARK.md](FORECAST_BENCHMARK.md) and [SIMULATOR_REALISM.md](SIMULATOR_REALISM.md); the short form is repeated beside each table below.

## 2. Detection

### Held-out result (20 unseen networks, original simulator)

| Metric | Mean | 95% interval of the mean | Min to max over networks |
|---|---|---|---|
| Precision | **0.82** (0.816) | 0.78 to 0.85 | 0.71 to 0.92 |
| Recall | **0.93** (0.932) | 0.90 to 0.96 | 0.82 to 1.00 |
| F1 | **0.87** (0.868) | 0.84 to 0.89 | 0.78 to 0.96 |
| Precision at 10 | 0.85 | 0.81 to 0.89 | 0.70 to 1.00 |
| Vacant houses still flagged | 54% (0.537) | | |

The intervals are Student-t intervals computed from the 20 per-network values in `evals/results/detection.json` (a percentile bootstrap of the same values agrees to within 0.01). The JSON itself stores only the mean and range, so these intervals are derived, not stored. They measure how much the result moves from one random network to the next. They say nothing about how far the simulator is from reality.

Pooled over the 220 thefts, 205 were flagged (0.932).

### By kind of theft

| Kind | Thefts | Caught | Recall | Pattern label correct |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Meter stopped | 43 | 42 | 0.98 | 1.00 |
| Hook bypass | 131 | 127 | 0.97 | 0.95 |
| Gradual tampering | 46 | 36 | **0.78** | **0.15** |

Gradual tampering is the weak case twice over: it is caught less often, and when it is caught the system labels it a gradual decline only 15% of the time (7 of 46), so a brief usually calls it a hook bypass.

### Threshold sweep (mean over the 20 networks)

| Flag threshold | Precision | Recall | F1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.4 | 0.784 | 0.973 | 0.867 |
| **0.5 (used)** | 0.816 | 0.932 | 0.868 |
| 0.6 | 0.879 | 0.845 | 0.856 |
| 0.7 | 0.952 | 0.518 | 0.645 |
| 0.8 | 0.933 | 0.323 | 0.457 |
| 0.9 | 0.725 | 0.114 | 0.193 |

F1 is flat from 0.4 to 0.6, so the choice among those is a choice of trade-off, not of quality. 0.50 was fixed on the development seeds and favours recall, because a missed theft costs more than a wasted visit. Past 0.7 recall collapses: only about a third of thefts reach HIGH confidence (recall 0.32 at 0.8).

### What this replaced

| Version | Precision | Recall | F1 | Source | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| First API metrics | 0.78 | 0.85 | n/a | git history, commit `99205c5` | **Hardcoded numbers, never measured.** On the demo network the live queue surfaced 7 of the 14 injected thefts (recall 0.50) while the API reported 0.85 |
| New scoring, no confidence cap | 0.79 | 0.96 | 0.87 | `99205c5` message | Measured on 20 held-out networks |
| **Current: cap at 0.75 without readable transformer evidence** | **0.82** | **0.93** | **0.87** | `evals/results/detection.json` | Measured on 20 held-out networks |

The cap (commit `ae368e0`) is the one component change with a recorded before and after. Without a readable transformer balance a theft and a vacant house look identical from the meter alone, so such meters now top out at MEDIUM. It moved about three points from recall to precision and left F1 unchanged. That is the intended effect: fewer wasted visits at the cost of a few thefts that stay in REVIEW.

The more important difference from the baseline is not a number: the first version reported accuracy it had not measured. Every figure now shown in the application is read from these files or computed against ground truth.

### Sensitivity to the simulator

The committed result uses the original simulator. Re-running on the simulator calibrated against real households gives lower numbers:

| Run | Precision | Recall | F1 | Gradual recall | Gradual label correct | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Held-out seeds 1000 to 1019, original simulator | 0.82 | 0.93 | 0.87 | 0.78 | 0.15 | `evals/results/detection.json` |
| Development seeds 0 to 19, calibrated simulator | 0.77 | 0.84 | 0.79 | 0.63 | 0.32 | [SIMULATOR_REALISM.md](SIMULATOR_REALISM.md); reproduced (0.766 / 0.836 / 0.794) |
| Held-out seeds 1000 to 1019, calibrated simulator | 0.77 | 0.86 | 0.81 | 0.70 | 0.35 | `python evals/detection_eval.py --simulator calibrated --networks 20 --first-seed 1000`, reproduced while writing this page (0.769 / 0.859 / 0.808); **not stored in `evals/results`** |

So the realism change costs about 5 points of precision and 7 of recall. It is the closest this repository gets to an answer on "how much of this is the simulator being easy", and it is still short of real data.

Note for maintainers: `evals/detection_eval.py` has defaulted to the calibrated simulator since commit `5c92d75`, but the committed `detection.json` was produced earlier, on the original. CI and `scripts/validate.sh` call the script without `--simulator`, so their recall gate (0.85) now runs against the calibrated simulator, where mean recall is 0.859. That passes with a margin under 0.01.

### Ablation

There is **no per-layer ablation** in the repository (no run with L0, L2 or L3 switched off). What exists:

- The confidence-cap comparison above.
- Unit tests that pin the mechanisms the layers are meant to provide: a theft with a transformer gap is flagged HIGH, a vacancy without a gap is not flagged, theft and vacancy on the same transformer are told apart, and a theft too small to see in the balance is reported as inconclusive rather than cleared (`backend/tests/test_scoring.py`).
- By construction L3 contributes at most 0.10 to a confidence, so it cannot change a flag on its own.

A real ablation would need to be added to `evals/` and is listed under limitations.

## 3. AI features

### Rules baseline (no model key)

From `evals/results/ai-rules.json`, run 2026-10-07, seeds 2000 to 2002.

| Measure | Result |
|---|---|
| Inspection brief, correct cause | **73%** (30 of 41) |
| Inspection brief, theft versus genuine call correct | **85%** (35 of 41) |
| Copilot, correct answers, as scored by the script | **80%** (24 of 30; see below for why this is generous) |
| Copilot, answers naming a meter that does not exist | **0** |
| Copilot median latency | 1 ms |

Brief accuracy by true cause:

| True cause | Cases | Correct | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Meter stopped | 6 | 6 | 1.00 |
| Hook bypass | 17 | 13 | 0.76 |
| Vacancy (should read as genuine drop) | 12 | 10 | 0.83 |
| Gradual tampering | 6 | 1 | **0.17** |

The rules brief inherits the detector's pattern label, so it fails where the label fails: gradual tampering is usually reported as a hook bypass. Of its six theft-versus-genuine mistakes, four are hook-bypass thefts explained as a genuine drop (the costly direction: a real theft would be waved through) and two are vacant houses called a hook bypass. All five gradual-tampering misses were called hook bypass, which is still the right theft call.

Copilot: the rules path answers a fixed set of question shapes. Six of 30 were marked wrong: "highest unmetered share" (twice), "list the flagged meters in a zone" (three times; the rules path returns a transformer balance sentence instead of a list) and "how many are high risk" (once). The pass criterion is a substring match, and it is generous: three of the 24 passes are accidents (two "how many are high risk" answers contain the expected digit only inside "48" or a rupee amount, and one transformer answer contains the expected id only inside the canned help text). Without those the rules baseline is about 21 of 30, nearer 70% than 80%. The headline 80% is what the script reports and is kept as the committed figure; the stricter reading is derived from the per-case rows in the JSON.

### Agent (language model) variants

**No agent results are committed, so none are claimed.** The agent evaluation runs in CI only when a model key secret is set, and no run output was saved to `evals/results/`. The design bounds what an agent can do wrong (fixed cause set, read-only tools, rules fallback) and the unit tests exercise those bounds with a scripted model, but whether the agent beats the rules baseline on cause accuracy is **not measured here**.

### How this differs from the alternative

The alternative to "rules decide, models explain" is a model that decides. That was not built or scored, so there is no head-to-head number. The reason for the choice is structural: detection is scored against ground truth at 0.82 / 0.93 by deterministic code and can be rerun exactly, and the model layer is scored separately on a closed set of causes.

## 4. Feeder forecast

Real London households summed 50 at a time into 20 pseudo-feeders; 28 rolling daily origins each, 560 day-ahead forecasts; nothing fitted on the scored days. Lower is better. Full table and caveats: [FORECAST_BENCHMARK.md](FORECAST_BENCHMARK.md). Source: `evals/results/forecast_benchmark.json`.

| Model | WAPE | MASE |
|---|---|---|
| Chronos-Bolt small (pretrained) | 9.9% | 0.73 |
| Chronos-Bolt tiny (pretrained) | 10.1% | 0.75 |
| **Seasonal mean of last 4 weeks (shipped)** | **11.2%** | **0.83** |
| Yesterday | 13.1% | 0.97 |
| Same slot last week | 13.3% | 0.98 |
| Previous app model (trend + weekly + monthly blend) | 20.5% | 1.52 |

How it differs from what it replaced and from the alternatives:

| Comparison | Change |
|---|---|
| Shipped seasonal mean against the previous model | MASE 1.52 to 0.83 (45% lower), WAPE 20.5% to 11.2% |
| Shipped model against a plain weekly seasonal-naive forecast | MASE 0.98 to 0.83 (16% lower); MASE below 1 means it beats seasonal-naive |
| Chronos-Bolt small against the shipped model | MASE 0.83 to 0.73 (11% lower). Not shipped: it needs PyTorch (hundreds of MB) and does not fit the 512 MB server. Available as `FORECAST_MODEL=chronos` with automatic fallback |

The 80% band (10th to 90th percentile of the model's own errors over the last two weeks) covered 78.7% of actual demand against a nominal 80%.

Provenance of the "previous model" row: it is recorded in `docs/FORECAST_BENCHMARK.md`, was measured once before the model was replaced, and is **not in the JSON** and not reproducible from the current tree. It was run on half-hourly data, so its 96-slot trend window did not match and the gap is probably a little exaggerated.

## 5. Simulator realism

Real households from the London dataset: 1,000 (every fifth), one 112-day Monday-aligned window each, split by shard so that calibration (shard 498) and scoring (shard 499) never share a household. Ten scale-free features (variability, autocorrelation, weekend ratio, night and evening share, load factor, skew, low-day ratio, intraday variance). Source: `evals/results/realism.json`.

| Simulator | Quality score | Column shapes | Pair trends | Real-vs-simulated AUC | Distance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Original | 60.9% | 32.4% | 89.4% | 1.00 | 0.902 |
| Calibrated (eight knobs, random search plus local refinement) | **83.6%** | 76.6% | 90.6% | **0.98** | 0.357 |

Quality is the SDMetrics report score (higher is closer). AUC is a gradient-boosting classifier trying to tell real from simulated households: 0.5 means it cannot, 1.0 means trivially. Distance is a scaled Wasserstein distance (lower is closer).

What changed: the marginal shapes of the features moved a long way (column shapes 32% to 77%, distance down 60%). What did not: a classifier still separates the two sets almost perfectly (AUC 0.98). The simulator is closer, not realistic. The effect of that on detection is in section 2.

## 6. How the results differ from baselines, in one table

| Area | Baseline | Now | Difference | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Detection reporting | Hardcoded 0.78 / 0.85; live queue found 7 of 14 thefts | Measured on 20 unseen networks: 0.82 / 0.93 / 0.87 | Unmeasured claim replaced by a reproducible measurement | commit `99205c5`, `detection.json` |
| Detection, confidence cap | No cap: 0.79 / 0.96 / 0.87 | Cap: 0.82 / 0.93 / 0.87 | +0.03 precision, -0.03 recall, F1 equal | commits `99205c5`, `ae368e0` |
| Detection on a more realistic simulator | Original simulator 0.82 / 0.93 / 0.87 | Calibrated 0.77 / 0.86 / 0.81 (held-out, reproduced) | About 5 points precision, 7 recall lower | section 2 |
| Brief cause accuracy | Not applicable (rules are the baseline) | 73% cause, 85% theft vs genuine | Agent not measured | `ai-rules.json` |
| Forecast | Previous blend, MASE 1.52 | Seasonal mean, MASE 0.83 | 45% lower | `FORECAST_BENCHMARK.md` |
| Forecast ceiling | Seasonal mean 0.83 | Chronos-Bolt small 0.73 | 11% lower, not shipped | `forecast_benchmark.json` |
| Simulator realism | Original: quality 61%, AUC 1.00 | Calibrated: quality 84%, AUC 0.98 | Closer, still separable | `realism.json` |

## Limitations and what did not work

- **Everything detection-related is simulated.** Theft patterns are authored by the same project that wrote the detector. A detector can learn the author's habits. The calibrated-simulator rerun shows the gap is not zero, and no real theft data was available to measure the rest.
- **The transformer input in the simulator is the true load plus a modelled loss.** That is what lets the balance layer separate theft from vacancy. Real transformers have metering error, unmetered legitimate load and varying technical loss, none of which is modelled beyond a loss band.
- **Vacant houses still look like theft about half the time (54%).** That is the main false-alarm source, and the reason every flag is meant to go through a brief and a field check, not an accusation.
- **Gradual tampering is the weakest case.** Recall 0.78 and a correct label 15% of the time on the original simulator; recall 0.63 and a label correct 32% of the time on development seeds with the calibrated one. A reworked hinge-ramp shape classifier scored 0.12 pattern accuracy and was dropped.
- **The baseline window is the first 14 days of history.** A theft that starts inside it contaminates its own baseline, and long-run drift is judged against day one. The evaluation starts thefts on day 18 or later, so it does not test this.
- **No per-layer ablation and no external baseline detector.** The repository shows what the full system does, not how much each layer contributes, and it does not compare against a z-score-only or published detector on the same networks.
- **Confidence intervals are about random networks, not about reality**, and they are derived from per-network values rather than stored.
- **The agent (language model) variants have no committed results.** Only the rules baseline is measured.
- **The copilot rules path fails on six of thirty questions**, and the eval's substring check is generous: three of the 24 passes are accidental, so the real rules score is nearer 70% than 80%.
- **Thresholds are not retrained from inspection outcomes.** Outcomes are recorded and shown; nothing learns from them.
- **The first API returned hardcoded metrics** and a first scorer found 7 of 14 injected thefts. Both were replaced; they are listed in [errorlog.md](errorlog.md).
- **The forecast is London data, day-ahead only**, with no weather or Indian holiday inputs. The 1.52 figure for the model it replaced is a one-off measurement that cannot be reproduced from the current tree.
- **Rupee figures use flat assumed tariffs** (domestic 6, industrial 8, commercial 9 per kWh) and the ROI page rests on stated assumptions, not billing data.
- **The simulator is closer to real homes but separable from them** (AUC 0.98, `shape_jitter` at its bound, weekend behaviour not copied, London not Bengaluru).

## Reproduce

```bash
python evals/detection_eval.py --simulator original --networks 20 --first-seed 1000   # committed detection.json
python evals/detection_eval.py --simulator calibrated --networks 20 --first-seed 1000 # sensitivity row (not stored)
python evals/ai_eval.py --mode rules                                                  # ai-rules.json
python evals/ai_eval.py --mode agent --delay 2                                        # needs GROQ_API_KEY
python evals/realism_eval.py                                                          # realism.json (downloads the London data once)
python evals/forecast_benchmark.py --chronos tiny,small                               # forecast_benchmark.json (needs torch, chronos-forecasting)
```
